text.p: Princeton Mining Corp said on Thursday it wants to acquire a mine or advanced exploration project to help boost its cash flow.

"We would be interested in something like an operating mine or a project well into the feasibility stage," Princeton Chief Executive Bill Myckatyn told reporters after the mining company's annual meeting.

Princeton would consider gold or base metals opportunities in North and South America and potentially Australia, he said. Such an acquisition would generate cash flow for the company and expand its size.
The company's Huckleberry copper mine in British Columbia, slated to begin production in September, will not generate meaningful free cash flow for some time because of a high debt load.
Princeton owns 60 percent of the project and the rest is held by four Japanese companies -- Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Dowa Mining Co Ltd, Furukawa Co Ltd and Marubeni Corp.
The C$137 million mine is expected to produce an average 65 million pounds of copper a year over the first 10 years of its 16-year life.

Myckatyn said that Huckleberry was three-quarters finished and construction had not been delayed by a legal challenge by an environmental group and local Indians on environmental grounds. A decision is pending in the case, but the company does not anticipate its permit will be revoked.
Princeton said that it expected it would take 3-1/2 to six years to repay its debt on Huckleberry, depending on the degree to which its Japanese partners exercised a right to additional cash flow.

Princeton is also seeking to do a reverse 5-for-1 share split but wants to coincide the move with a "good news" development at the company, Myckatyn said. Such a consolidation would be aimed at making the shares more attractive to institutions.

Turmoil in the share market for small mining stocks after the Bre-X Minerals Ltd debacle had delayed Princeton's plan to spin off partial ownership of its Chilean exploration properties, Myckatyn said. The company still intends to issue equity in its Aquest Minerals Corp subsidiary that holds the properties but the timing is unclear.

At its Similco copper mine in British Columbia, operations are likely to remain suspended for the rest of the year. The mine was shut last November due to a slump in copper prices and high development costs for ore in the Copper Mountain area of the property.
Princeton is considering three options for the property -- closing it permanently, restarting it or exploring the idea of enlisting a partner to restart the operation.
